29.0.s.en: 1. The righteous and the concept of authority

29.0.0.en: 1 He, that being often reproved hardeneth his neck, shall suddenly be destroyed, and that without remedy. 2 When the righteous are in authority, the people rejoice: but when the wicked beareth rule, the people mourn. 3 Whoso loveth wisdom rejoiceth his father: but he that keepeth company with harlots spendeth his substance. 4 The king by judgment establisheth the land: but he that receiveth gifts overthroweth it. 5 A man that flattereth his neighbour spreadeth a net for his feet. 6 In the transgression of an evil man there is a snare: but the righteous doth sing and rejoice. 7 The righteous considereth the cause of the poor: but the wicked regardeth not to know it. 8 Scornful men bring a city into a snare: but wise men turn away wrath. 9 If a wise man contendeth with a foolish man, whether he rage or laugh, there is no rest. 10 The bloodthirsty hate the upright: but the just seek his soul. 11 A fool uttereth all his mind: but a wise man keepeth it in till afterwards. 12 If a ruler hearken to lies, all his servants are wicked.

29.0.1.en: He, that being often reproved hardeneth his neck, shall suddenly be destroyed, and that without remedy [1].

29.0.2.en: Wise Solomon has already praised the rebuke that comes from a heart full of fatherhood or brotherhood, sincere in its love and faithful in its concern for the one it rebukes. He considered such rebuke better and more profitable than honeyed words and than praise given in a spirit of flattery. But if the rebuke comes from a hard neck or an arrogant soul, it does not offer a remedy, but causes wounds that cannot be healed and fractures that cannot be set.

29.0.3.en: On the other hand, rebuke, even if it comes from a loving heart, and even from God Himself, if a person hardens his heart, becomes a cause of his judgment and not of his healing. This is what happened to many, such as Pharaoh in the days of Moses the prophet, Ahab and Jezebel in the days of Elijah, and many of the kings of Israel after the division.

29.0.4.en: * Judge, O bishop, with authority like that of God. But whoever repents, receive him to yourself, for God is the God of mercy.

29.0.5.en: Rebuke the one who sins, and teach with cheerfulness the one who does not wish to return to you.

29.0.6.en: Didascalia, chapter 3 * There must be true standards for our words and teachings, so that they may not take on the appearance of excessive leniency or exaggerated harshness.

29.0.7.en: * In this office it does not befit the shepherd to be harsh and violent, nor to be too lax, lest in the first case he be like one with unjust authority, and in the second like one who without cause dishonors the office he has received.

29.1.0.en: St. Ambrose When the righteous are in authority, the people rejoice: but when the wicked beareth rule, the people mourn [2].

29.1.1.en: The righteous often resort to firmness and not to laxity with the reckless and the negligent, while the wicked may not care about what their subordinates do. But the righteous leader, with all his firmness, pours a spirit of joy upon the community, whereas the wicked leader causes groaning and bitterness for his subordinates.

29.1.2.en: * At the birth of the saints joy spreads among all, for it is a blessing to everyone.

29.1.3.en: * There is a special joy at the beginning of the conception of the saints and at their birth, for the saint does not only gladden his family, but becomes a cause of the salvation of many. This phrase (Lk 1:14) teaches us to rejoice at the birth of the saints.

29.1.4.en: St. Ambrose * I will offer you proof of what I say in the case of a king.

29.1.5.en: Saul the son of Kish did not covet kingship, but was only seeking his donkeys. He went to Samuel the prophet to ask him about the donkeys, and the prophet told him of God's calling for him to set him up as king. Yet Saul did not hasten to accept, but drew back. But when he used his authority as king in an evil way, this authority that was given to him by God, was his drawing back enough to protect him from the wrath of God who had granted him this kingship? Was he able to say to Samuel when he rebuked him: Did I rush and hasten to accept authority? I wanted to live as one of the common people in a life full of peace and without disturbance. But it was you who compelled me to accept. If you had left me in my simple (lowly) state, I would not have fallen into all these stumblings, but I would have remained unknown among the people, and consequently I would not have been sent to this battle, and God would not have entrusted me with the war against Amalek... and so I would not have sinned.

29.1.6.en: But such excuses are feeble; they are not merely feeble but dangerous, for in truth they kindle the wrath of God.

29.1.7.en: For whoever thinks of himself that he is not responsible for error, because he has received a work that the common people have not received, is like one who protests the love of God as a reason for his own personal errors.

29.1.8.en: St. John Chrysostom * Let a man know his own measure, so that no one may dare to take for himself the office of shepherding while vice still dominates him and causes his condemnation. For one whom iniquities have corrupted ought not to intercede for the iniquities of others.

29.2.0.en: Whoso loveth wisdom rejoiceth his father: but he that keepeth company with harlots spendeth his substance [3].

29.2.1.en: The Book of Proverbs invites us to enter into a relationship of love with wisdom: "Love her, and she shall keep thee" (Prov 4:6), and here it says: "Whoso loveth wisdom rejoiceth his father" (Prov 29:3). And in the Book of Wisdom it is said: "I became a lover of her beauty" (Wis 8:2). He enters, as it were, into a spiritual wedding relationship!

29.2.2.en: Whoever enters into friendship with harlots squanders his wealth and ruins his life. Therefore the Apostle advises us: "Flee also youthful lusts" (2 Tim 2:22). He also says: "What? know ye not that he which is joined to an harlot is one body?... But he that is joined unto the Lord is one spirit" (1 Cor 6:16-17). Whoever is joined to a harlot loses everything, but whoever is joined to the Lord enjoys unity with Him, and the heavenly Father rejoices in him as his parents rejoice in him.

29.2.3.en: * If anyone obeys Solomon and takes true wisdom as his companion and the partner of his life, of whom he says: "Love her, and she shall keep thee" [exalt her, and she shall promote thee] (cf. Prov 4:6, 8), he prepares himself for this love, keeping the wedding garment pure, rejoicing in this wedding, so that he may not be cast out, since he is wearing what is fitting for one who is married. It is clear that the longing for this kind of wedding is shared by men and women alike. For the Apostle says: "There is neither male nor female" (Gal 3:28), and Christ is all to all human beings. The aim of the true lover of wisdom is to cling to God, the true Wisdom, the incorruptible Bridegroom, and so he has the love of true wisdom, that is, of God.

29.2.4.en: St. Gregory of Nyssa * In my opinion the picture of the soul that longs to keep the blessed tradition without losing a single point sometimes runs like this: "When a man loves wisdom, he rejoiceth the heart of his father." Wells that are constantly used supply us with purer water, but wells from which no one draws become foul. Use makes iron brighter, and disuse makes it produce rust. In general, use (work) makes souls and bodies healthy.

29.3.0.en: St. Clement of Alexandria The king by judgment establisheth the land: but he that receiveth gifts overthroweth it [4].

29.3.1.en: Bribery corrupts the foundations of laws and destroys the land, so we must hate it as an enemy of ours (Prov 15:27). It corrupts justice (Prov 17:23). By a bribe a person can reach the great (Prov 18:16), and win their favor (Prov 19:6), but it causes disputes and robs a person of his peace (Prov 21:14).

29.3.2.en: The righteous King of kings alone came to turn our earth into heaven, and to grant the leaders to enjoy fellowship with Him, so that they may establish truth, justice and righteousness. But whoever seeks gifts as a bribe, and whose heart clings to material things, corrupts the judgment.

29.3.3.en: * No one was able to know Wisdom, for "no man knoweth the Son, but the Father; neither knoweth any man the Father, save the Son, and he to whomsoever the Son will reveal him" (Mt 11:27). Therefore He revealed Him to John, since Wisdom was with the Apostle, and he spoke not what was according to his own thought, but what Wisdom had poured into him: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God" (Jn 1:1). In truth death could not hold her, for Wisdom said: [O death, where is thy victory? O death, where is thy sting?] (cf. 1 Cor 15:55).

29.4.0.en: St. Ambrose A man that flattereth his neighbour spreadeth a net for his feet [5].

29.4.1.en: Although everyone needs words of encouragement, if praise turns into flattery as a kind of courtesy, adulation or amusement, it is like a net spread out into which the person falls.

29.4.2.en: * "The righteous shall chasten me with mercy, and reprove me: but let not the oil of sinners anoint my head" (Ps 140:5).

29.4.3.en: The oil of the sinner is the expressions of flattery and fawning; these the prophet hates greatly. He loves that the righteous man should rebuke him and discipline him with sternness and mercy, and does not want praise with hypocrisy and partiality. For fawning and adulation profit a person nothing, but increase his ignorance and iniquity and his persistence in them...

29.4.4.en: God said through the prophet: "O my people, those who call you blessed lead you astray" (Isa 3:12), that is, those who praise you and speak of you with tales out of hypocrisy and deceit only deceive you and destroy you utterly. But those who rebuke you and counsel you do you a great kindness.

29.4.5.en: * (Laxity toward sinners) is not a virtue but a weakness. It is neither love nor meekness but neglect; indeed it is cruelty toward those souls that are overlooked, so that they perish without being warned of their ruin.

29.5.0.en: St. Augustine In the transgression of an evil man there is a snare: but the righteous doth sing and rejoice [6].

29.5.1.en: It is fitting for us to distinguish between the fall of the wicked and the fall of the righteous. The first falls, and surrenders to the fall, and so is shattered, but the second, even if he falls, rises. Therefore even after his fall he sings and praises God, who forgives sin and rescues souls from corruption. The language of the wicked is frustration and despair; the language of the righteous is hope, joy and rejoicing in the Lord.

29.5.2.en: * ["Jesus answered them, Verily, verily, I say unto you, Whosoever committeth sin is the servant of sin" (Jn 8:34).]

29.5.3.en: He is a servant, would that it were of a man, but of sin!

29.5.4.en: Who is not terrified before such words? May the Lord our God grant us, you and me, that I may speak in fitting terms about this freedom, seeking it, and that I may avoid that bondage...

29.5.5.en: What a wretched bondage! When human beings suffer from wicked masters, they seek by all means a change of master. What does the servant of sin do? To whom does he present his request? From whom does he seek salvation...?

29.5.6.en: Where does the servant of sin flee? For he carries (his mistress, that is, sin) wherever he flees. The evil conscience does not flee from itself; there is no place for it to go.

29.5.7.en: Indeed he cannot withdraw from himself, for the sin he commits is within him. He commits sin in order to obtain some bodily pleasure. But the pleasure passes and the sin remains. What he delights in passes, and the sting remains behind it. What an evil bondage...!

29.5.8.en: Let us all flee to Christ, and appeal against sin to God as our Savior.

29.5.9.en: Let us ask to be sold, so that He may save us by His blood. For the Lord says: "Ye have sold yourselves for nought; and ye shall be redeemed without money" (Isa 52:3). You shall be saved without a price on your part; so says the Lord, for He paid the price, not with money but with His blood, otherwise we would have remained needy slaves.

29.5.10.en: * This world is without doubt the valley of tears in which a man sows while weeping. It supports you to continue in your faith. In any case, explain what this book means by the seed that we sow now.

29.5.11.en: It is the good works which God has ordained for each one of us to walk in (Eph 2:10). And He planned for us to perform them by the power of His Spirit in the midst of the toils of this troubled life.

29.5.12.en: Whoever learns to practice the work of God in this world, this valley of tears and toils, becomes joyful like the diligent farmer who sows the seed even in the death of winter; can the cold winds and harsh weather keep him from his work? Certainly not! So it is fitting that we look at the troubles of this life. Amusements are thrown in our way by the evil one, with the aim that we may turn aside from the good works which we were created to do. See what the Psalmist says: "He that goeth forth weeping..." Truly he finds reason for weeping; each one of us finds it. Yet we must go on, practicing the good works of God along our way.

29.5.13.en: How wretched we would be if we had been called to work earnestly only to weep, without looking for any fruit of our labor. How wretched we would be if we found no one to wipe away our tears.

29.5.14.en: But we know that the Holy Spirit works that we may continue planting in the midst of our tears. For through the Psalmist the Spirit promises us that we shall return astonished with joy! We bring the fruit of our labor as an offering to Him.

29.6.0.en: St. Augustine The righteous considereth the cause of the poor: but the wicked regardeth not to know it [7].

29.6.1.en: Since the righteous is occupied with his brethren, he hears the voice of the poor, responds to his groans, and recognizes his complaint. But the wicked shuts his heart upon the "ego," and seeks only what he thinks is for his personal benefit; thereby he loses true knowledge.

29.6.2.en: * Mercy is a universal virtue, and the basic principle that must be practiced everywhere and by every age, so that neither the Pharisee nor the soldier nor the farmer is exempt from it... neither the rich nor the poor, for all are called to give to those who have not, because mercy is the perfection of the virtues.

29.7.0.en: St. Ambrose Scornful men bring a city into a snare: but wise men turn away wrath [8].

29.7.1.en: The scornful man counts his success in stirring up differences among those around him, appearing as one who wishes to reconcile them and spread peace among them, or who works for their benefit, as Demetrius the silversmith did, who made silver shrines for Diana (Acts 19:23-41). But the wise man finds his peace in the peace of his brethren; he turns away wrath from himself, as he turns it away from his brethren, so that all may live in the true peace of God.

29.7.2.en: * St. Nilus of Sinai made a comparison between these two measures of virtue in the cases of the blessed Moses the prophet and his brother Aaron: the rite of covering the chest and the heart with the priestly breastplate, which Aaron performed when he entered the Holy of Holies, represented the state of the person who, though angry in his heart, suppresses this anger by struggle and prayer. But the state of the person who has no anger at all in his heart, because he has reached perfection by his victory over the passions and demons, St. Nilus compares with what was said of Moses the prophet, saying: "Moses the prophet offered the breast as a sacrifice, because the soul dwells in the heart, and the heart in the breast."

29.7.3.en: And wise Solomon says: "Wise men turn away wrath" (Prov 29:8), and the Scripture says regarding Aaron: "And thou shalt make holy garments for Aaron thy brother for glory and for beauty. And thou shalt speak unto all that are wise hearted, whom I have filled with the spirit of wisdom, that they may make Aaron's garments to consecrate him, that he may minister unto me in the priest's office... a breastplate, and an ephod, etc. And thou shalt put in the breastplate of judgment the Urim and the Thummim; and they shall be upon Aaron's heart, when he goeth in before the LORD" (Ex 28:2-4, 30). This teaches us monks that it is fitting for us to cover the anger of the heart with good, humble, quiet thoughts, and not to allow anger to rise to the throat, where the tongue exposes the stench of this anger.

29.7.4.en: * Abba Moses said: "He who humbly bears a word of injustice or reproach for the sake of Christ completes his martyrdom, and he who becomes poor for God's sake, God provides for him, and he who shows his weakness before God or becomes foolish for His sake, God makes wise."

29.7.5.en: Paradise of the Fathers * When the peace of the mind is struck by anger, it grieves and tears it, like one who falls into confusion, so that it is not in harmony with itself, and loses the power of its inner harmony. Let us then take into consideration how grave the sin of anger is, by which we lose gentleness, the likeness to the image of the Most High. By anger wisdom is driven out, and we are left in complete ignorance of what to do and how to do it.

29.8.0.en: If a wise man contendeth with a foolish man, whether he rage or laugh, there is no rest [9].

29.8.1.en: It is hard for a fool to realize his errors and confess them, for he is always stiff-necked in his opinions, thinking that he is right in everything. So if a wise man tries to guide him, whether with firmness or gentleness, he will not accept his guidance and advice.

29.9.0.en: The bloodthirsty hate the upright: but the just seek his soul [10].

29.9.1.en: The violent, hard-hearted person who sheds blood hates the upright man, because the latter condemns him, if not openly then through his conduct, which pricks the conscience of the wicked. The first example in the life of mankind is therefore Cain, who killed his brother Abel, for no reason except that he offered a sacrifice acceptable to God (Gen 4:5). But the person who loves virtue finds rest in the upright man and clings to him.

29.9.2.en: * Sitting with those who are not wise shatters the heart, and conversing with the virtuous is a sweet spring.

29.9.3.en: * Do not descend to the slack, or you will put yourself in the lowest rank, but let your converse be with lovers of good, that you may dwell with them on high. Therefore let your abode be bravely in the places where there is the highest knowledge. Go to the city of light, and do not descend to the sinners.

29.10.0.en: St. Isaac the Syrian A fool uttereth all his mind: but a wise man keepeth it in till afterwards [11].

29.10.1.en: The foolish man is ready to look for any reason to rage and be furious against others, without regard for the consequences of his wrath. But the wise man is patient, and even if he is stirred within himself over some act, he does not hasten until he calms down, and examines the situation with deliberation and without agitation.

29.10.2.en: Haman was foolish and stupid, for he found a reason to kill an entire people because he imagined that one of the members of this people did not honor him and bow down to him as to a god. But King David wisely looked for a reason to calm himself against his opponents, so he refused to take revenge on King Saul, and he listened to Abigail and praised her because she kept his hand from shedding the blood of her husband Nabal.

29.10.3.en: * We ought to restrain every movement of anger and soften it under the guidance of discernment (wisdom), so that we may not rush headlong in blind fury, of which Solomon said: "A fool uttereth all his mind: but a wise man keepeth it in till afterwards" (Prov 29:11). That is, the foolish man blazes up with the passion of anger to avenge himself, but the wise man, because of the maturity of his counsel and his gentleness, extinguishes anger little by little and rids himself of it.

29.10.4.en: The Apostle says something similar: "Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord" (Rom 12:19). That is, do not allow your hearts to be confined in the narrow straits of impatience and cowardice, so that when any violent storm of anger rises you cannot bear it, but let your hearts be wide, receiving the waves of angry words into the wide streams of love, which "beareth all things... endureth all things" (1 Cor 7:13). Thus your minds will be enlarged with longsuffering and patience, and in it will be the depths of faithful counsel that faces the smoke of anger and destroys it.

29.10.5.en: The phrase can be understood in the following sense: we give place to anger to the extent that we submit with a humble and quiet mind to the passion of others, and bow to the impatience of those who are in turmoil, as though we deserved every kind of wrong (as a discipline for us).

29.10.6.en: But those who distort the meaning of the perfection of which the Apostle speaks, interpreting giving place to wrath as keeping away from a person at the time of his anger, seem to me by this not to cut off the causes of anger but to stir up the motives of strife. For unless we immediately set right the anger of our neighbor with a correction full of humility, keeping away provokes the neighbor all the more...

29.10.7.en: Solomon speaks of such a matter, saying: "Be not hasty in thy spirit to be angry: for anger resteth in the bosom of fools" (Eccl 7:9). And "Go not forth hastily to strive, lest thou do something to the other when thy neighbour hath put thee to shame" (Prov 25:8). By this he does not blame haste in quarrel in the sense that he praises delayed quarrel.

29.10.8.en: In the same way we must understand the saying: "A fool's wrath is known in his day: but he that covereth shame is prudent" (Prov 12:16), for it does not mean that the wise man stores up the outburst of anger secretly, but it blames the rash outburst of anger... He must hide the outburst for this reason, that while he leaves it for a time the spirit of anger subsides forever. For this is the nature of anger: when room is left for it (that is, when we do not hasten with it) it weakens and perishes, but if anger is exposed in a state of turmoil it burns more and more.

29.10.9.en: Hearts must be enlarged and opened so that they are not confined in the narrow straits of cowardice and filled with increasing anger, and become able to receive the commandments of God by what the prophet calls "largeness of heart" or "surpassing largeness." For the prophet says: "I will run the way of thy commandments, when thou shalt enlarge my heart" (Ps 119:32). For slowness to anger is wisdom, which we learn by the clear sayings of the Holy Bible. For "He that is slow to wrath is of great understanding: but he that is hasty of spirit exalteth folly" (Prov 14:29). Therefore the Holy Bible says of the person who asked the Lord for the gift of wisdom: "And God gave Solomon wisdom and understanding exceeding much, and largeness of heart, even as the sand that is on the sea shore" (1 Kgs 4:29).

29.10.10.en: Father Joseph * Let the one who is not gentle listen to the saying of the Holy Bible: "He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city" (Prov 16:32). Victory over cities is of less importance, because what is subdued here is something external, but victory by means of gentleness is a far greater act, because it is the mind that conquers and rules itself by itself, when gentleness compels the mind to control itself inwardly.

29.10.11.en: Let the angry man understand what the Truth says to His chosen ones: "In your patience possess ye your souls" (Lk 21:19). The way of creation is indeed a wonderful matter, for the mind governs the soul, and the soul rules the body. But the soul loses its rule over the body if the mind does not rule over it. Therefore the Lord shows us that gentleness is the guardian of our states, and teaches us also that by gentleness we can possess ourselves. Thus we understand the gravity of the sin of lack of gentleness (that is, anger) when we see that by it we lose our very being (our existence).

29.10.12.en: Let the angry hear what Solomon says: "A fool uttereth all his mind: but a wise man keepeth it in till afterwards" (Prov 29:11). It is through the impulse of anger that the spirit is entirely laid bare, and it inclines to anger more quickly, because wise inner discipline is not available. But the wise man holds back and leaves future matters to care for themselves. And when someone wrongs him he does not rush to take vengeance at once, because by his forbearance he desires not to lose the others, although he truly knows that all things will be punished by a just judgment on the last Day of Judgment.

29.10.13.en: On the other hand, we should exhort the gentle man not to let his heart be grieved by what he suffers outwardly. For this great sacrifice which such persons offer without any hindrance ought not to be spoiled by any infection of inner malice. For even if people do not see their grief, the searching divine eye sees it.

29.11.0.en: If a ruler hearken to lies, all his servants are wicked [12].

29.11.1.en: The wicked ruler or leader in any community represents a focus that includes wicked people who share his evil, and by their evil counsel they push him all the more toward evil. When Jeroboam and all Israel asked Rehoboam the son of Solomon to lighten the yoke upon them, he consulted young men who were not wise, and answered: "My little finger shall be thicker than my father's loins... my father chastised you with whips, but I will chastise you with scorpions" (2 Chr 10:10-11), and the kingdom was divided, and ten tribes withdrew from him.

29.11.2.en: * A foolish counselor is a blind guard, and a wise counselor is a fortress of confidence.

29.12.0.en: 13 The poor and the deceitful man meet together: the LORD lighteneth both their eyes. 14 The king that faithfully judgeth the poor, his throne shall be established for ever.

29.12.1.en: The poor and the oppressor meet together.

29.12.2.en: The LORD lighteneth both their eyes [13].

29.12.3.en: By the oppressor here he means the usurer who exploits the poor, who lends to the poor at interest without regard for their circumstances and capabilities. It would have been fitting for him to realize that the One who gave the poor man the light of life is the very One who gave him the same light. For God is the source of life of both, and it is He who will judge between them.

29.12.4.en: * You have begun to belong to a great family, and by this kinship all become brothers: master and servant, commander and soldier, rich and poor. Christians have earthly fathers of different ranks and classes, some of them noble and some despised, and yet they all call upon one heavenly Father, they all say: "Our Father which art in heaven." Have they understood that they are brothers? Let the master not disdain to regard his servant as a brother, looking to our Lord Jesus who granted him to be a brother to him.

29.12.5.en: By love alone the children of God are distinguished from the children of the devil.

29.12.6.en: * By love alone the children of God are distinguished from the children of the devil.

29.12.7.en: A man can be baptized and born again, but let him look into his heart and see whether he loves his brother; then he can truly say: "I am a son of God." Otherwise, even though he has received the mark of the sacrament, he is no better than a deserter from the army and a vagabond.

29.13.0.en: St. Augustine The king that faithfully judgeth the poor, his throne shall be established for ever [14].

29.13.1.en: The one who judges with justice and cares for the poor and needy is upheld by divine providence, so his kingdom is established, and blessing comes upon his children and grandchildren.

29.13.2.en: * Let us sow those good seeds generously, so that we may reap generously in due season. Now is the time for sowing, where I ask you not to neglect it, so that in the time of harvest we may gather the fruits of what we have sown here, and enjoy the tender compassion from the Lord.

29.13.3.en: * If you invite a friend, he continues to thank you until the evening, but friendship lasts for a time and ends very quickly, and does not equal what it cost you in expense. But if you invite a poor or maimed person, the thanks does not spoil, for God remembers it for you eternally, He will not forget it, since He Himself becomes your debtor.

29.14.0.en: 15 The rod and reproof give wisdom: but a child left to himself bringeth his mother to shame. 16 When the wicked are multiplied, transgression increaseth: but the righteous shall see their fall. 17 Correct thy son, and he shall give thee rest; yea, he shall give delight unto thy soul. 18 Where there is no vision, the people perish: but he that keepeth the law, happy is he. 19 A servant will not be corrected by words: for though he understand he will not answer. 20 Seest thou a man that is hasty in his words? there is more hope of a fool than of him. 21 He that delicately bringeth up his servant from a child shall have him become his son at the length. 22 An angry man stirreth up strife, and a furious man aboundeth in transgression. 23 A man's pride shall bring him low: but honour shall uphold the humble in spirit. 24 Whoso is partner with a thief hateth his own soul: he heareth cursing, and bewrayeth it not. 25 The fear of man bringeth a snare: but whoso putteth his trust in the LORD shall be safe. 26 Many seek the ruler's favour; but every man's judgment cometh from the LORD. 27 An unjust man is an abomination to the just: and he that is upright in the way is abomination to the wicked.

29.14.1.en: The rod and reproof give wisdom: but a child left to himself bringeth his mother to shame [15].

29.14.2.en: Parents who do not care for the upbringing of their child ruin his soul and shatter his character, and he becomes a shame and disgrace to them. Rebuke and discipline given with wisdom and love support the child to enjoy wisdom.

29.14.3.en: Eli the priest neglected the upbringing of his two sons, so they perished and he perished with them, and the ark of the covenant was lost from the people, and the army was defeated.

29.14.4.en: * Discipline (or rebuke) is a sign of loving care, and it leads to understanding.

29.14.5.en: The Teacher shows this rebuke when He says in the Scripture: "How often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not!" (Mt 23:37). And the Scripture also says: "They went a whoring after idols and stones, and offered their burnt offerings to Baal." It is a great proof of His love, for although He knows the shame of those who rejected Him and that they ran far away from Him, yet He urges them to repent. And Ezekiel says: [But thou, son of man, be not afraid to speak to them; perhaps they will hear] (cf. Ezek 2:6). And He says to Moses: "Go and tell Pharaoh to let my people go. But I know that he will not let them go." Here both things appear: His divinity, which is shown by His foreknowledge of what will happen, and His love, by giving them the opportunity to choose repentance for themselves. And in His care for the people He rebuked them through Isaiah, saying: "This people honour me with their lips, but their heart is far from me" (Isa 29:13). And He says also: "But in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men" (Mt 15:9). Here His loving care shows their sins and salvation side by side.

29.14.6.en: St. Clement of Alexandria When the wicked are multiplied, transgression increaseth.

29.15.0.en: But the righteous shall see their fall [16].

29.15.1.en: The wicked think that they are successful and have obtained authority, but soon righteousness prevails, and the righteous see the wicked fallen.

29.15.2.en: * Just as the saint is the temple of God, so the sinner makes of himself a tomb.

29.15.3.en: St. Jerome * Those who are not saints die in their sins, but the saints repent of them. They bear their wounds and recognize their errors. Then they go to the priest seeking a remedy, or seek cleansing by the bishop.

29.15.4.en: Origen * Although the servants and friends of God avoid the sins that lead to death, and practice many good works, we do not believe that they are without trivial sins, for God does not lie, where it is said: "No infant whose life is one day upon the earth is without sin." The blessed John the Evangelist, who is without doubt no less than James in worthiness, added to this: "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us" (1 Jn 1:8). Moreover, we read in another place: "For a just man falleth seven times, and riseth up again" (Prov 24:16).

29.16.0.en: Father Caesarius, Bishop of Arles Correct thy son, and he shall give thee rest; yea, he shall give delight unto thy soul [17].

29.16.1.en: Whoever disciplines his son finds rest in due time, and reaps joyful fruits and delights that gladden the soul.

29.16.2.en: * A father does not train his son if he does not love him, and a good teacher does not correct his pupil unless he sees in him signs of obtaining the promise. When the physician withdraws his care from a patient, this is a sign of his despair of his healing.

29.16.3.en: * Which is better: that we enter a battle (of discipline) for a time and carry stakes of thorn (skewers of stakes), and have weapons with us, and are wearied by carrying heavy shields, so that afterward we may rejoice through victory, or that we remain slaves forever, because we could not endure for a single hour?

29.17.0.en: St. Jerome Where there is no vision, the people run wild: but he that keepeth the law, happy is he [18].

29.17.1.en: By vision is meant inner insight, true seeing, and knowledge of the word of the Lord. As it is said: "And the word of the LORD was precious in those days; there was no open vision" (1 Sam 3:1). But the leader who responds to the word of the Lord and keeps the commandment, his eyes are opened and he enjoys a blessed life that is reflected on those whom he guides and shepherds.

29.17.2.en: * The Scriptures (the Holy Bible) are an ocean in which you find the hidden pearl.

29.17.3.en: So the interpreter must dive into the water to bring it out.

29.17.4.en: The mind dives into the Scriptures, brings out the pearl, and shows it to the merchants.

29.17.5.en: And the mind dives into the Torah, and seizes the divine pearl.

29.17.6.en: And the tongue offers it to the hearers, saying: Fasten the daughter of light in your minds as an adornment for yourselves.

29.17.7.en: St. Jacob of Serugh * It is very beneficial to read the Holy Bible, for it makes the soul wise, directs the spirit toward heaven, moves a person to thanksgiving, destroys the desire for earthly things, and lets our minds constantly contemplate the other world.

29.18.0.en: St. John Chrysostom A servant will not be corrected by words: for though he understand he will not heed [19].

29.18.1.en: The Septuagint has "the stubborn servant." The stubborn person, full of malice, cannot have his affairs set right by gentle, kind speech, for he needs some firmness. For even if he realizes the gravity of his conduct, he does not care, because of his stubbornness.

29.18.2.en: Some see that in our stubbornness we often need God's firmness and His disciplines for us, as He did with Jonah when he insisted on disobedience, so God allowed the sea to rage against him and for him to be thrown into the sea, and at the same time He prepared a great fish for him and rescued him.

29.18.3.en: * By saying: "A servant will not be corrected by words," (Solomon) does not command that (the servant) be left to himself, but counsels the means that must be used for correction. Otherwise he would not have said: "Will not be corrected by words." For he says in another place that not only the servant but also the undisciplined son must be corrected by beating, and so he bears great fruit. For he says: "Thou shalt beat him with the rod, and shalt deliver his soul from hell" (Prov 23:14).

29.18.4.en: St. Augustine Seest thou a man that is hasty in his words?

29.19.0.en: There is more hope of a fool than of him [20].

29.19.1.en: Wisdom requires slowness in speech, so that we speak only after listening to the other party, and weigh matters with deliberation before we utter a word.

29.19.2.en: Jephthah was hasty in uttering his vow, and so he sacrificed his only daughter (Judg 11:21). Herod was hasty in his promise to his brother's daughter, and so he killed St. John the Baptist (Mt 14:8-11). King Saul was hasty in his judgment, and almost killed his son Jonathan had it not been for the intervention of the people (1 Sam 14). The Apostle James advises us: "Let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath" (Jas 1:19).

29.19.3.en: * As long as a man lets himself talk on without restraint, the gravity of silence flees from him, and he loses the safe keeping of himself. Therefore it is written: "The work of righteousness shall be quietness" (Isa 32:17). So Solomon says: "A city broken down and without walls is the man who hath no rule over his spirit in speech" (Prov 25:28) [Vulgate]. He also says: "In the multitude of words there wanteth not sin" (Prov 10:19). And the Psalmist bears witness to this, saying: "A talkative man shall not be established on the earth" (Ps 140:11), and indeed the value of a true statement is lost when it is spoken without discernment...

29.19.4.en: A true statement is against the wicked, if it aims at the benefit of the good... But the wicked cannot hear good words with patience, ignoring the reform of their lives, so they attach themselves to words in order to answer others.

29.19.6.en: * Beware of the chattering tongue and the ears eager to hear news. Do not belittle others, and do not listen to one who belittles others.

29.19.7.en: * The garrulous old woman, the old man who speaks fables, and the sophist in his words, all these seize the Holy Scriptures and tear them into pieces, and they may teach with them without having learned them.

29.20.0.en: St. Jerome He that delicately bringeth up (pampereth) his servant from a child shall have him become grateful at the length [21].

29.20.1.en: Whoever pampers his servant from his youth, that is, spoils him, and does not bind him to obligations and the sense of responsibility and work, in the end he becomes "grateful," that is, the master is obliged to be very grateful to his servant. Some translate it "he becomes a son," that is, he inherits his possessions as a son. Though our father Abraham esteemed the person and services of Eliezer of Damascus, he could not bear that he should inherit him in place of having a son of his own.

29.20.2.en: This proverb can be interpreted as a call not to pamper the body, since it is a servant of the soul and its slave, and not a master over it who moves it with fleshly lusts and pleasures. This is what led the Apostle Paul to say: "I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection" (1 Cor 9:2).

29.20.3.en: The Lord Christ called us to be counted children of God, although we are His servants. Therefore the free love of God, His surpassing grace and His wonderful works with us call us not to be proud even if we do what is right, but to say "We are unprofitable servants" (Lk 17:10).

29.20.4.en: * When Israel was formed from its childhood and was surrounded and pampered with delights and luxury... "he waxed fat, and grew thick," until (the Israelites) finally fell into captivity among the Gentiles. The man who is pampered in his childhood is handed over to slavery.

29.21.0.en: St. Ephrem the Syrian An angry man stirreth up strife, and a furious man aboundeth in transgression [22].

29.21.1.en: The angry man causes quarrels and strife, so it is fitting for us to flee from anger and fury, lest we fall into hatred and enmity. It is also fitting for us to avoid the angry man, especially when he is angry, and not to answer his anger with anger. The elder son in the parable of the compassionate father and the prodigal son became angry, and so he insulted his father, wronged his brother, and deprived himself of entering his father's house (Lk 15).

29.21.2.en: * Whoever is angry is empty of longsuffering and love, quickly troubled by trivial words, and stirs up strife over a small, paltry matter, and wherever he has no place he throws himself in... Who does not mourn for such a man? He is despised by God and men.

29.21.3.en: St. Ephrem the Syrian * An elder said: He whose brother quarrels with him, and his heart is not grieved, has become like the angels. If he quarrels with him and then returns at that very hour and reconciles with him, this is the work of strugglers. But the one who grieves his brethren and is grieved by them, and holds on to malice in his heart, is obedient to Satan and opposes God, and God does not forgive his offenses unless he forgives his brethren.

29.22.0.en: The Garden of the Monks A man's pride shall bring him low: but honour shall uphold the humble in spirit [23].

29.22.1.en: When the proud man is puffed up he falls, and when the humble man walks in a spirit of meekness he receives honor from God and men. As St. Mary said: "He hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree" (Lk 1:52).

29.22.2.en: * It is clear that excessive boasting was among the marks of the false apostles.

29.22.3.en: * Haughtiness together with sin is a great calamity... If the one who does good loses his labor if he is puffed up, how great is the iniquity of him who adds to his sins the sin of haughtiness? For such a one cannot practice repentance.

29.22.4.en: St. John Chrysostom * As soon as you become proud you immediately lose what you have received.

29.22.5.en: St. Augustine * Whoever loves humility acquires many gifts through humility.

29.22.6.en: When you seek mercy, you find it in the humble, for humility is the dwelling place of righteousness.

29.22.7.en: Teaching is found with the humble, and knowledge is the springs of their lips.

29.22.8.en: Humility begets wisdom and understanding, and the humble acquire prudence...

29.22.9.en: Sweet is the word of the humble, and his face is radiant, and he laughs and rejoices.

29.22.10.en: Love is beautiful among the humble, and they know how to manage with it.

29.22.11.en: The humble fast from all evils, and their faces shine with the goodness of their hearts.

29.22.12.en: The humble man speaks and his speech is fitting, and his lips laugh, yet the sound of his laughter is not heard...

29.22.13.en: The humble man is humbled, but his heart is lifted up to the heights above. Where his treasure is, there are his thoughts. The eyes of his face look to the earth, and the eyes of his mind to the heights above.

29.22.14.en: St. Aphrahat Whoso is partner with a thief hateth his own soul.

29.23.0.en: He heareth cursing, and bewrayeth it not [24].

29.23.1.en: Whoever shares with the thief what he has stolen, even if he did not carry out the act of theft, shares in his crime, and falls with him under the sentence. It is dangerous to share in the sins of others, in one way or another, or to cover for them, without urging them to repent and turn back from their evil. The Law pronounced judgment against one who conceals stolen goods (Lev 5:1). And John the Apostle says: "If there come any unto you, and bring not this doctrine, receive him not into your house, neither bid him God speed: for he that biddeth him God speed is partaker of his evil deeds" (2 Jn 10-11). And Paul the Apostle also says: "Neither be partaker of other men's sins" (1 Tim 5:22).

29.24.0.en: The fear of man bringeth a snare: but whoso putteth his trust in the LORD shall be safe [25].

29.24.1.en: It is fitting for us to fear God and not to fear men, and as St. Arsenius asks us to be servants of one Master, and not to enslave ourselves to many masters.

29.24.2.en: The Apostle Paul says: "For do I now persuade men, or God? or do I seek to please men? for if I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ" (Gal 1:10). The Lord Christ says: "And I say unto you my friends, Be not afraid of them that kill the body, and after that have no more that they can do. But I will forewarn you whom ye shall fear: Fear him, which after he hath killed hath power to cast into hell" (Lk 12:4-5).
